questions.text:
The diagram below shows a river system consisting of 7 segments, marked P, Q, R, S, T, U, and V. It splits the land into 5 zones, marked Z1, Z2, Z3, Z4, and Z5. We need to connect these zones using the least number of bridges. Out of the following options, which one is correct?
Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.solution:
This problem can be solved by representing the map as a graph:

- Each zone is represented as a vertex. - Each river segment where a bridge can be built is represented as an edge connecting the adjacent zones.

The graph is as follows:

River Segment Adjacent Zones
P Z1- Z2
Q Z1- Z3
R Z2- Z3
S Z1- Z5
T Z3- Z5
U Z5- Z4
V Z3- Z4

We have 5 vertices (zones). To connect all zones with the minimum number of bridges, we need a spanning tree, which always contains

[latex] n-1=5-1=4 [/latex] edges.

Now check each option.

Option A: Bridges on P, Q, and T
Only 3 bridges are used, so all 5 zones cannot be connected.
Incorrect.

Option B: Bridges on P, Q, S, and T
The selected edges are:
- P : Z1-Z2 - Q : Z1-Z3 - S : Z1-Z5 - T : Z3-Z5

Zone Z4 is not connected.
Incorrect.

Option C: Bridges on Q, R, T, and V
The selected edges are:
- Q : Z1-Z3 - R : Z2-Z3 - T : Z3-Z5 - V : Z3-Z4

Every zone is connected, and there are exactly 4 bridges (forming a spanning tree).
Correct.

Option D: Bridges on P, Q, S, U, and V
Uses 5 bridges, whereas only 4 are required for a minimum spanning connection.
Incorrect.

options: Bridges on P, Q, and T
Bridges on P, Q, S, and T
Bridges on Q, R, T, and V
Bridges on P, Q, S, U, and V

questions.text:
In the given figure, PQRS is a square of side 2 cm and PLMN is a rectangle. The corner L of the rectangle is on the side QR. Side MN of the rectangle passes through the corner S of the square.

What is the area (in [latex]cm^{2} [/latex]) of the rectangle PLMN?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.solution:
Set up coordinates matching the figure: [latex]P=(0,2),\ Q=(0,0),\ R=(2,0),\ S=(2,2)[/latex] (square side [latex]2[/latex]). Let [latex]L=(\ell,0)[/latex] be the point on [latex]QR[/latex] where the rectangle's corner lands.

Side [latex]PL[/latex] has direction vector [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex] and length [latex]\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. Since [latex]PLMN[/latex] is a rectangle, side [latex]LM[/latex] is perpendicular to [latex]PL[/latex], along direction [latex](2,\ell)/\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. If the rectangle's width (side [latex]LM[/latex]) is [latex]h[/latex], then:
[latex]N=P+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}},\qquad M=L+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex]

Since side [latex]MN[/latex] must pass through [latex]S=(2,2)[/latex], substituting [latex]S[/latex] into the line through [latex]M,N[/latex] (which runs parallel to [latex]PL[/latex], direction [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex]) and solving the resulting two equations simultaneously gives:
[latex]h=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex]

So the rectangle's area is:
[latex]\text{Area}=PL\times LM=\sqrt{\ell^2+4}\times\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}=4[/latex]

Remarkably, this is independent of [latex]\ell[/latex] — the area comes out to exactly [latex]4[/latex] regardless of where [latex]L[/latex] sits on [latex]QR[/latex], as long as [latex]MN[/latex] passes through [latex]S[/latex].

Answer: 4

questions.text:
Which one of the following options is correct for the given data in the table?
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Iteration} (i) & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline \text{Input} (I) & 20 & -4 & 10 & 15 \\ \hline \text{Output} (X) & 20 & 16 & 26 & 41 \\ \hline \text{Output} (Y) & 20 & -80 & -800 & -12000 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
questions.solution:
Testing the proposed recurrences directly against the table:

[latex]X(i)=X(i-1)+I(i)[/latex]: [latex]X(1)=20+(-4)=16[/latex] ✓, [latex]X(2)=16+10=26[/latex] ✓, [latex]X(3)=26+15=41[/latex] ✓ — matches the [latex]X[/latex] row exactly.

[latex]Y(i)=Y(i-1)\times I(i)[/latex]: [latex]Y(1)=20\times(-4)=-80[/latex] ✓, [latex]Y(2)=-80\times10=-800[/latex] ✓, [latex]Y(3)=-800\times15=-12000[/latex] ✓ — matches the [latex]Y[/latex] row exactly.

Answer: X(i)=X(i-1)+I(i); Y(i)=Y(i-1)×I(i); for i>0

questions.text: If IMAGE and FIELD are coded as FHBNJ and EMFJG respectively then, which one among the given options is the most appropriate code for BEACH?
questions.solution:
Comparing each letter's position to its coded counterpart across both examples reveals the rule: reverse the word, then shift every letter forward by one position in the alphabet. Check: IMAGE reversed is EGAMI; shifting each letter [latex]+1[/latex] gives FHBNJ — matches exactly. FIELD reversed is DLEIF; shifting [latex]+1[/latex] gives EMFJG — matches exactly.

Applying the same rule to BEACH: reversed is HCAEB; shifting each letter forward by [latex]1[/latex]: H→I, C→D, A→B, E→F, B→C, giving IDBFC.

Answer: IDBFC

questions.text:
Based only on the conversation below, identify the logically correct inference:

"Even if I had known that you were in the hospital, I would not have gone there to see you", Ramya told Josephine.
questions.solution:
The sentence "Even if I had known that you were in the hospital, I would not have gone there to see you" is a counterfactual conditional — the phrase "even if I had known" (past perfect, hypothetical) directly implies that Ramya did not, in fact, know that Josephine was in the hospital at the time. The sentence only tells us what Ramya claims she would have done in that hypothetical scenario, not anything about their friendship history or the reason Josephine was hospitalized.

Answer: Ramya did not know that Josephine was in the hospital.
